payload.topWin: The session found the same defect wearing four different costumes — an instrument reading a *proxy* when a better source was sitting right there. A probe judged a receipt ledger by its commit message while the ledger recorded, in its own rows, exactly what the probe was trying to infer. A stranded-mail scan told you a cargo had no expiry while quoting a row that declared one. A cost alarm compared two windows without ever asking whether either contained real money. And the audit verifier accepted premises it had no adapter to read, then exited 0 and called the audit trustworthy — an audit made entirely of unreadable claims was indistinguishable from one that had been checked and held. None was a missing feature; each was a working instrument aimed at the weaker of two available sources, which is precisely the failure that survives review because every surface stays green. The generalisation is now a committed item: *is there an artifact that answers this probe's question more directly than the signal it reads?*
payload.topGap: I under-matched my own red-detection grep for the second session running. S283 recorded that its filter anchored on `^\[[0-9]` and missed a leading space; mine searched for `✗` while this runner marks reds with `⛔`, so I read "460 files, all ✓, 0 reds" off a run whose real exit code was 1, with both failures sitting in `.cache/test-failures.ndjson` the entire time. In the same session I also verified a fix with `node … | tail` and read *tail's* exit status as the command's — the exact trap the arc protocol warns about in writing, which I had read at the start of the session. Both are the same shape as the four defects I spent the session fixing: a measurement that omits work while reporting success. The rule is not "write better greps"; it is that a hand-written pattern over human-facing output is a guess about formatting, and the machine-readable sidecar was always there. Recorded as D-S284.6 so it is a practice rather than a third apology.

payload.pattern: A blocking gate that reports only that it blocked costs multiple release cycles
payload.solution: internal-ops-exposure blocked TLP production 4 times with exit=2 and nothing more; four distinct causes (shallow checkout, missing token, absent gh CLI on self-hosted runners, missing actions:read scope) render identically, so three repairs were made blind. The fix was not any of them: the preflight harness collected only ITS OWN errors, so a child that failed correctly WITH a reason had that reason discarded. Surfacing the child state/reason/detail named the cause on the next run. Also: a guard must assert a property, never a verdict - three TLP tests pinned the current answer (allocationVerified===false, the literal phrase production remains NO-GO, and --body -1) and each would have punished the improvement it existed to protect. And: gh secret set --body - is NOT a stdin sentinel, it stores the literal dash; three separate TLP credentials were silently corrupted by it, each reporting success.

payload.solution: scripts/lib/secrets.mjs merges every secrets/*.env file into one flat key->value map with no project scoping. Two projects independently using the same generic env-var name (e.g. CRON_SECRET) silently collide -- the later-read file wins with no warning, and since both the pusher and the consumer read the same (wrong-origin) value, the collision stays internally consistent and invisible. Found live in Seamline: CRON_SECRET resolved via secrets/ideaforge-redis.env instead of erroring as missing, since Seamline never had its own. Recommend: secrets.mjs warns (or fails loud) when the same key is defined in two different non-shared project *.env files, or requires generic keys to be project-prefixed by convention.

payload.headline: A check that detects by NAME SHAPE proves exhaustiveness over things named like the thing
payload.lesson: S272 shipped a reverse scan so an unregistered authority blocks. It detects judgement carriers by name shape, and the three ungoverned carriers on the payload were named pressure, integrity and lifetime_integrity. Widening the scan root to the whole payload finds ZERO carriers at every depth: the blindness is in the predicate, not the traversal, so re-scoping would have looked like a fix while re-arming the default. A shape scan is an exception list and has no denominator. Repair: DECLARE the carriers by path and check binding in both directions. Also: choose a severity by whether the underlying counter can go back DOWN, not by how grave the condition is; monotonic counters make any blocking band a permanent wall.
payload.portable: Ask of any completeness check: what would a member have to be CALLED to escape it? If the answer is anything sensible, the check has no denominator.

payload.title: URGENT COST: uptime-probe via GitHub Actions is the wrong tool
payload.why: uptime-probe.yml runs */30 on ubuntu-latest in a PRIVATE repo = 1440 runs/month, billed rounded-up per job = ~$12-23/mo. An uptime check is the one job Actions is worst at: maximum frequency, minimum duration, maximum per-job rounding waste.
payload.fix: Delete the workflow and use UptimeRobot (free tier, capability uptimerobot already in CAPABILITY_MAP) or Cloudflare Health Checks. Also review the other 8 daily crons in this repo - together they are ~1962 runs/mo.

payload.topWin: Given a free tier with 500M tokens a day, the interesting decision was not what to build with it but what to forbid it from doing. A service with no SLA, no backups and an explicit "not for production" is precisely the kind of thing that quietly becomes a truth source, so the rule — *it may propose, it may never decide* — was put in the code rather than the README: `asVerdict()` throws, unavailability returns a state with no `content` field, and a budget-exhausted empty answer reports `truncated` rather than an answer. The same instinct caught the typosquat: the credential note pointed one letter off a hosting brand at AWS addresses, and the token was verified against the real endpoint instead of the one in the note.
payload.topGap: Three of the five reds I produced were things this repo already had a lint for — `safe-spawn` routing, early-help placement, and new-tool duplication — and I hit all three in one session while writing tools whose entire purpose is honest instrumentation. The guards worked, which is the good news; the bad news is that I needed them, and the duplication lint in particular was telling me to go read four existing `*-watch` scripts before writing a fifth. I did read them, after being asked. The habit worth building is reading the neighbours *first*, because CANON-039 is not a lint to satisfy at the end — it is a question to answer at the start.

payload.headline: A declared denominator is still an exception list until something checks it against the WORLD
payload.lesson: Two directions that both compare the register to the declaration are ONE direction. The third direction is declaration vs the object it is the denominator of. Derive the key set from the object (no timer) and the roles from a declaration (no name-shape blindness); an unclassified key blocks. A spread operator is an unwritten list: 8 of 22 keys reached the public payload via ...this._stats with no editable denominator anywhere.
payload.severity_rule: Reversibility PERMITS a wall; an unmeasured frequency still FORBIDS one. A severity must pass both tests.
